categories.g2: What the words on the agenda mean

entrees.definition: The mayor and the 24 ward councillors, meeting together. It is the body that adopts by-laws, the budget and the big decisions.
A smaller group of councillors that studies one field (planning and housing, transit, finance, audit…) before Council. It hears the public, debates and recommends. Most decisions are shaped there.
What a committee asks Council to do. When Council “carries” the item, the recommendation becomes the decision. “As amended” means Council or the committee changed the wording first.
A proposal put to a vote, moved by one member and seconded by another. Ottawa numbers them (2026-88-01: meeting 88, first motion). A motion can add, change or delay a decision.
Carried: the majority said yes. Lost: the majority said no. When there is no recorded vote, the minutes keep only the result, not who voted how.
Council took note of a report without deciding anything: an audit, an update, a plan “for information”. Nothing is approved and nothing is refused.
A vote where each member’s name is written down with a yes or a no. It is how the minutes show how your councillor voted.
On a vote without a recorded tally, the minutes can note that a member disagreed. “Carried with dissent from Councillor X” means it passed and X was against.
An instruction a member gives to City staff during a meeting, recorded in the minutes: study something, report back, add an option. It is not a by-law.
A municipal law. Zoning, parking, noise, fees, taxes: all by-laws. Council often adopts several by-laws together at the end of a meeting.
A change to what can be built on a given piece of land: height, number of homes, use. Most planning decisions are this. The address and ward are in the title.
The City’s long-term map of where and how Ottawa should grow. A zoning change that contradicts it needs an Official Plan amendment too.
Protecting a building under Part IV of the Ontario Heritage Act. Changes to a designated building then need the City’s approval under that Act.
Items nobody wants to debate, adopted together in a single vote. Any member can pull one out to discuss it. Many routine decisions pass this way.
A part of the meeting closed to the public, for subjects the law allows, such as legal advice, land deals or personnel. The minutes name the subject, not the content.
A member announces a motion for the next meeting, so everyone can read it first. Nothing is decided yet.
Council agrees to set aside its usual procedure rules, for example the notice period, to decide something right away. The minutes record the motion that does it.
A written question from a member to staff (OCC-2026-18…). The answer comes back at a later meeting, as a memo. It is information, not a decision.
“ACS2026-PDB-RHU-0049 – Kanata North (Ward 4)”: the department’s file number, then the ward the decision touches. “City-wide” means it touches everyone.

The money for running the City every day: salaries, buses, snow, libraries. It is paid mostly by property taxes, fees and transfers from other governments. Our reading of the 2026 draft is on the Budget tab.
The money for building and repairing things that last: roads, pipes, arenas, buses. Often paid with debt and reserves rather than this year’s taxes.
What the province’s assessment agency (MPAC) says your property is worth. Your municipal tax is this value times the City’s tax rate.
Money set aside for a purpose: stabilize taxes, replace buses, cover a bad winter. The budget shows each reserve’s opening and closing balance.

Council lets staff sign contracts and make routine decisions without a vote, within limits set by by-law. The City publishes the contracts of $25,000 or more awarded this way. That list is our Contracts tab.
A contract awarded without a competitive process, with a written reason: only one supplier can do it, an emergency, a follow-on to an existing contract. The reason is in the City’s list.
